title: Mira Murati's Team Open-Sources a Model That Thinks Three Times Before Speaking: 26.4B Recurrent Transformer Tops Hugging Face and Runs on a Laptop

content_html:
Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab has given the industry a public lesson in a new architecture. The company released the open-weight model Inkling2Mini, which uses a looped Transformer architecture—the model has 24 layers in total, with the middle 12 layers running three times for each token, while the first and last six layers each run only once. The beauty of this design is that the model can extend its "internal thinking" without generating more text, thinking through an answer with fewer tokens—essentially letting it think more and say less. Previously, the same-series Inkling2Small had 594B parameters and was considered too large; this time it was cut directly to 26.4B, small enough to fit on a laptop.

Its scorecard is quite impressive. The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index gives it 20.1 points, placing it on the Pareto frontier of intelligence and active parameters; ARC Prize officially reported 49.3% on ARC-AGI-2 at $0.14 per task, and 84.5% on ARC-AGI-1 at only $0.06 per task; in coding, it scores 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 77.9% on SWE-Bench Pro v2Hard, the highest among models of the same size. As an MoE architecture, its active parameter count varies slightly depending on the source; the official comparison table lists 5.4B/26.4B activated/total parameters. The model supports text and image input, with a context window stretched to 1M tokens.

The sincerity of the open-source release also shows in the deployment barrier. The model releases full weights and a variable-loop research version under the Apache 2.0 license. It can run locally on a Mac with 32GB or more memory and also run on NVIDIA DGX Spark; vLLM provides Day-0 support, and the Ollama pre-release can launch it with a single command; Unsloth even offers an extreme compression solution—after 1-bit quantization, it needs only 9GB of memory. Within hours of release, it reached #1 on the Hugging Face trending list.

The biggest question raised by looped architectures is whether "the model spinning in its head" is still visible. This approach of hiding reasoning inside multiple loops naturally raises concerns that the thought process becomes unmonitorable. Thinking Machines took the opportunity to conduct a round of research: they found that as the number of loops increases, the model's no-CoT ability rises, its chain of thought becomes shorter but remains readable, and monitorability does not decline noticeably. The company also open-sourced a variable-loop research model for others to run their own experiments; NDIF hosts the model and variants, providing white-box access so users can intervene in the model's internals without their own compute, and offers a complete guide to cross-loop reading, patching, and steering activations.

This small 26B model showed off an offline trick on launch day—Mira Murati shared a case where the team used it offline on a plane to build a flight simulator. Coding, computer use, visual reasoning, finance, and other agentic tasks are all its home turf; in multiple comparisons on industry competitive benchmarks such as Vals Index and FrontierCode, it beat models including Gemma431B. As "stuffing reasoning into loops and models into laptops" becomes a new trend in the open-source community, Inkling2Mini may be just the opening chapter of the looped-architecture story.
